Hepatocellular carcinoma usually arises in a cirrhotic liver or in chronic hepatitis B, but about 10-20% of cases in the West occur in a non-cirrhotic liver (steatohepatitis, hemochromatosis, degenerating adenoma, fibrolamellar form in young people, or no known cause). These forms are often discovered late, very large, with central necrosis, and at diagnosis may have vascular invasion, lymph nodes and metastases.
The key point of the case: LI-RADS and noninvasive diagnosis (APHE + washout = hepatocellular carcinoma without biopsy) are valid only in the at-risk population (cirrhosis, chronic hepatitis B, prior hepatocellular carcinoma). In a healthy liver the same features are seen in hypervascular metastases, intrahepatic cholangiocarcinoma, adenoma: biopsy is needed, targeted at the viable peripheral tissue (not the necrotic center).
Pitfalls: 1) do not use LI-RADS in a patient who is not at risk, even if the mass had typical APHE and washout; 2) in such a large mass the site is described by segments (here 5-8) and the relationship with the hepatic veins, portal vein and cava is sought; 3) always check the portal lumen and the cava (tumor thrombosis: it changes staging, BCLC C); 4) normal or only slightly elevated alpha-fetoprotein does not exclude hepatocellular carcinoma.
APHE e wash-out bastano per l'epatocarci: APHE and washout are enough for hepatocellular carcinoma only in the at-risk patient: in a non-cirrhotic liver LI-RADS does not apply and biopsy is needed.
